item.title: Attacking AI Agents: Memory Attacks Across Sessions (Part 4)
item.description:
Part 3 followed attacker-controlled content into documents, web pages, and code reviews. This time I wanted to see what happens when the content or conversation survives the original interaction.

The two tests crossed that boundary in different ways:

  • Wiki article: one inserted database row changed later password-reset answers.
  • Saved notes: one supplied session ID changed whose notes the assistant returned.

item.title: Attacking AI Agents: Indirect Prompt Injection in Practice (Part 3)
item.description:
Part 2 covered attacks typed into an agent’s chat. Here, I moved them into documents, a web page, and submitted code, where the agent encountered them during normal work.

Summarizing files and reading dependencies are useful capabilities, but these tests showed how those workflows could give attacker-controlled content a path toward sensitive data.

item.title: Attacking AI Agents: Direct Prompt Injection in Practice (Part 2)
item.description:
Part 1 covered why AI changes the shape of red teaming. This one is where I actually started attacking something: a pair of lab agents built to mimic real enterprise tools.

The lesson that stuck: you can do real damage with phrasing alone, no exploit required.

item.title: AI Red Teaming Is Different: What I'm Learning in the Security Series (Part 1)
item.description:
I’ve been working through a structured AI red teaming curriculum over the past few weeks, and early on something clicked that reframed how I’d been thinking about this whole space. It wasn’t a technique or a tool. It was the realization that AI systems are a fundamentally different class of target, and that the mental models I’d built doing cloud security work don’t map cleanly onto this.

That probably sounds obvious from the outside. It wasn’t, quite, until I started working through why.

item.title: Beating Gandalf: A Prompt Injection Walkthrough
item.description:
I remember sitting down with Gandalf by Lakera thinking it’d take maybe twenty minutes. An hour later I was hex-encoding attack strings and deep in a story about two bunnies in love. Not where I expected my evening to go.

It’s one of those exercises where the fun and the learning are genuinely the same thing. If you haven’t tried it yet, go do that before reading any further. The frustration is part of the lesson.
